name: Electrical engineer
summary: Electrical and electronics engineering interviews usually test fundamentals you can apply: circuits, machines, power systems, electronics and protection, plus safety. Candidates commonly report questions on their project or internship, a technical test at many companies and, for experienced roles, questions on the equipment, panels or designs they've worked on. Electronics and communication roles lean more towards devices, digital logic and signals.
rounds: Online or written test: aptitude and electrical or electronics subjects (at many companies and campus drives)
Technical interview on core subjects, your project and internships
Practical questions for some roles, such as reading a circuit or a single-line diagram
For experienced roles, a discussion of the equipment, panels, designs or sites you've worked on
HR round, often covering site work, shifts and relocation
looks_for: Fundamentals explained simply: Ohm's law, AC and DC, power factor, machines
Safety first: isolation, earthing, lock-out and permits
Knowing protection devices and why they trip
Owning your project and internship work

questions.text: Tell me about your final-year project or internship. What did you build or test yourself?
covers: The problem and what the system did
Your own part: circuit design, components, coding or testing
The results, what failed along the way and what you'd change

questions.text: Tell me about a time you found the cause of a fault that others had missed.
covers: The symptom and what had already been tried
Your method: measurements, drawings, ruling things out
The cause, the fix and how you confirmed it

questions.text: Describe a time you followed, or insisted on, a safety procedure when it slowed the work down.
covers: The task and the risk
The procedure, such as isolation, lock-out or a permit, and any pressure to skip it
Why it mattered and how others responded

questions.text: Tell me about a circuit or design of yours that didn't work at first. How did you debug it?
covers: What went wrong
How you narrowed it down, step by step
The fix and the lesson you took into later work

questions.text: Explain power factor in plain words. Why do factories try to improve it?
covers: The share of current doing useful work, versus current that just flows back and forth
Low power factor means more current, bigger losses and often extra charges from the utility
Improving it with capacitor banks, without overcorrecting

questions.text: A motor trips soon after it starts. What would you check?
covers: Isolating it safely first
The supply: voltage, a missing phase, loose connections
The load and the motor: a jammed or overloaded machine, winding insulation, then the protection settings

questions.text: What's the difference between a fuse, an MCB and an RCCB? When does each one operate?
covers: A fuse melts on overcurrent and has to be replaced
An MCB trips on overload or short circuit and can be reset
An RCCB trips when current escapes to earth, protecting people from shock

questions.text: Why is power transmitted at high voltage over long distances?
covers: The same power at a higher voltage needs less current
Line losses grow with the square of the current, so they fall sharply
Transformers step voltage up for transmission and down for use

questions.text: How does a transformer work, and why won't it work on DC?
covers: A changing current in one winding makes a changing magnetic flux in the core
That flux induces a voltage in the other winding, scaled by the turns ratio
DC gives no change in flux, so nothing is induced and the winding just heats up

questions.text: Why is earthing important, and what could happen if an earth connection is poor?
covers: Earthing gives fault current a safe path so protection trips
A poor earth can leave metal parts live and protection may not operate
How earthing is tested and maintained

questions.text: Explain how diodes and transistors are used in a simple circuit, such as a phone charger or a switch.
covers: Diodes let current flow one way, so they turn AC into DC in a power supply
A transistor can act as a switch or an amplifier, controlled by a small input
An example from a project or lab

questions.text: What's the difference between analogue and digital signals, and why do so many systems convert to digital?
covers: Analogue varies continuously; digital uses discrete levels
Digital resists noise, is easy to store and process, and can be copied without loss
What conversion needs: sampling fast enough and enough resolution

questions.text: Why are many industrial sensors wired as a 4–20 mA current loop rather than a voltage signal?
covers: The current is the same all along the loop, so long cables don't distort the reading
The 4 mA 'live zero' shows a broken wire as a fault, not as a zero reading
Better resistance to electrical noise in plants

questions.text: You're asked to choose a cable size for a new machine. What would you need to know?
covers: The load current, voltage and how the machine starts
Length of run for voltage drop, how the cable is installed and the temperature around it
The protection device rating and the local standard you'd follow

questions.text: Tell me about yourself and what you've built or worked on outside class.
covers: Your degree and strongest subjects
A project, internship or hobby build that shows hands-on interest
The kind of role you want next

questions.text: Why electrical or electronics engineering, and which area do you want to work in?
covers: What draws you to the field, shown by an experience
An area such as power, design, maintenance, electronics or instrumentation
What you'd want to learn first

questions.text: Are you comfortable with site work, shifts or travel?
covers: An honest answer, with any limits stated clearly
Any site, plant or substation experience you have
How you'd handle on-call or shift work

tips: Revise circuits, machines, power systems, power electronics and protection; for ECE, add devices, digital electronics and signals.
Explain concepts with everyday examples: a ceiling fan motor, a phone charger, a substation you've passed.
In fault-finding questions, start with safe isolation, then work from supply to load in a logical order.
Know your project in depth: the circuit, the components you chose and why, and the test results.
Some companies that hire EEE and ECE graduates for software roles also test programming basics; check what the role needs.
If you did an internship at a plant or substation, be ready to describe the equipment and the safety rules you followed.
